title: Grieving an animal
hook: the loss of a pet is real grief

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was butsudan, a home altar where families tell their dead the news. Your line was a voice in memory: the bond continues, in a new shape.

The water bowl is still by the back door. Nobody has moved it, because moving it would make it true. The leash hangs on its hook. Fur keeps turning up on a dark sweater, weeks later, and each time it's a small shock. The house is too quiet at the hour when someone used to wait by the door. Then a coworker says, kindly enough, it was just a dog, you can get another one. And the grief, which was real a minute ago, suddenly has nowhere to go.
screen: `THE BOWL BY THE BACK DOOR.` → `THE QUIET HOUR.` → `"IT WAS JUST A DOG."`

segments.voice: First, what was lost. A life with an animal is built out of daily things: the feeding, the walk in the rain, the weight at the end of the bed, being greeted at the door as if you'd been gone a year. When the animal dies, a whole shape of the day goes with it. Second, a name for grief that others don't count. The grief researcher Kenneth Doka called it disenfranchised grief: a loss the people around you don't recognize as worth mourning, so there's no card, no time off, no one asking how you are. An animal's death can fall there. Naming it doesn't fix it, but it can explain why the sadness feels lonely. Third, old texts paid attention to animals. Proverbs says: "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast." And a psalm praises God's care stretching wide: "O LORD, thou preservest man and beast." Traditions give different answers about what becomes of an animal after death, and those answers belong to each tradition. The question of grief is simpler: was the love real? Fourth, a poet who didn't hide it. When Lord Byron's dog Boatswain died, he had a monument raised at his family home and wrote verses for the stone, calling the dog his friend. People have mocked grief for animals, and people have built monuments for it. Either way, it comes from the same place as grief for a person.
screen: `A WHOLE SHAPE OF THE DAY` · `GRIEF OTHERS DON'T COUNT` · `"MAN AND BEAST"` · `A POET'S MONUMENT TO A DOG` · then, large: `LOVE WAS REAL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind an animal you loved, your own, a childhood pet, a neighbor's dog that always came to the fence, and see one ordinary moment with them, the sound at the door, the warmth against your leg. Let yourself miss them, if you do, and silently say their name and one thing they gave you. If no animal comes to mind, think of one who belongs to someone you know, and how much that animal matters to them.
Disenfranchised grief, Kenneth Doka's name for a loss, like an animal's death, that others around you don't recognize as worth mourning. Today's word.
Your line: love was real. The bowl by the door can stay. That's day eight hundred one.

howItsDone: People mark the death of an animal in many ways: burying them in a garden, keeping a collar or a photo, planting something, or telling stories about them with family, and some vets and charities offer support for pet loss.

chat.says: My dog died and I can't stop crying. Is that silly? It was just a dog.
options: Not silly. A whole shape of your day is gone, and the love was real.
It's a bit much, since grief is really meant for people, not for pets.
It's fine, but getting a new puppy soon is the quickest way to stop it.
chat.meaning: Grief for an animal comes from the same place as grief for a person: a love that was real, and a daily life it shaped.

notes: Byron paraphrased, not quoted: the monument's prose inscription is sometimes attributed to John Cam Hobhouse, so the script credits Byron only with having the monument raised and writing verses calling the dog his friend. Verify.
'Traditions give different answers about what becomes of an animal after death' is deliberately general; no tradition's view is ranked.
The fork reveal says pet grief 'can be' the kind others don't count.
